articles.title: New software package: ERPLAB Studio
articles.content:
We are excited to announce the release of a new EEG/ERP analysis package, ERPLAB Studio. We think it’s a huge improvement over the classic EEGLAB user interface. See our cheesy “advertisement” video to get a quick overview.

Rather than operating as an EEGLAB plugin, ERPLAB Studio is a standalone Matlab program that provides a more efficient and user-friendly interface to the most commonly used EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines.

With ERPLAB Studio, you automatically see the EEG or ERP waveforms as soon as you load a file. And as soon as you perform an operation, you see what the new EEG/ERP looks like. For example, when you filter the data, you immediately see the filtered waveforms.

You can even select multiple datasets and apply an operation like artifact detection on all of them in one step. And then you can immediately see the results, such as which EEG epochs have been marked with artifacts.

We give you access to EEGLAB’s ICA-based artifact correction tools, but with a nice bonus. You can plot the ICA activations in the same window with the EEG data, making it easy to see which ICA components correspond to specific artifacts such as eyeblinks.

The program has an EEG tab for processing continuous and epoched EEG data, and an ERP tab for processing averaged ERPs.

The automatic ERP plotting makes it easy for you to view the data laid out according to the electrode locations. And we have an Advanced Waveform Viewer that can make publication-quality plots.

ERPLAB Studio is mainly just a new user interface. Under the hood, we’re running the same EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines you’ve always used. And scripting is identical.

ERPLAB Studio is included in version 11 and higher of ERPLAB. You simply follow our download/installation instructions and then type estudio from the Matlab command line.

If you’re new to ERPLAB, we strongly recommend that you go through our tutorial before starting to process your own data.

If you already know how to use the original version of ERPLAB (which we now call ERPLAB Classic), you can quickly learn how to use ERPLAB Studio with our Transition Guide.

We also have a manual that describes every feature in detail.
articles.author: Steve Luck

articles.title: Network Models of Neurodegeneration: Bridging Neuronal Dynamics and Disease Progression
articles.content: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by the accumulation of misfolded proteins and widespread disruptions in brain function. Computational modeling has advanced our understanding of these processes, but efforts have traditionally focused on either neuronal dynamics or the biological processes underlying disease. One class of models uses neural mass and whole-brain frameworks to simulate changes in oscillations, connectivity, and network stability. A second class focuses on biological processes underlying disease progression, particularly prion-like propagation through the connectome, glial responses and vascular mechanisms. Each modeling tradition has provided important insights, but experimental evidence shows these processes are interconnected: neuronal activity modulates protein release and clearance, while pathological burden disrupts neuronal function. Modeling these domains in isolation limits our understanding, although recent studies have begun to bridge the two by coupling neuronal and pathological processes. To determine where and why disease emerges, how it spreads, and how it might be altered, mathematical models that capture feedback between neuronal dynamics and disease biology are needed. This review surveys the two modeling approaches and highlights efforts to unify them, emphasizing that linking neuronal activity and disease progression is key to identifying strategies that slow, halt, or reverse degeneration and restore neural function.

articles.title: Optogenetics: Pinpoint Light on Precise Neuromodulation
articles.content: Optogenetics has emerged as a pivotal tool in neuroscience, enabling intricate modulation of targeted neurons within the nervous system. Despite its transformative potential, achieving high spatiotemporal resolution in neuromodulation remains a significant challenge, particularly in free-behaving animals. This review aims to highlight recent advances in optogenetic systems for neuromodulation, focusing on the efforts to achieve superior precision in spatiotemporal control. We provide a comprehensive overview of the breakthroughs in optogenetic tools that offer ultrafast responsiveness, strategies for targeted tissue- and cell-specific optogene delivery, and methods for precise optical stimulation with minimal impact on the behavior of subjects. Additionally, we review the applications of optogenetics in neurological diseases, emphasizing its potential to advance therapeutic interventions. These innovations are poised to propel optogenetics into a new era, accelerating its clinical translation for precision neuromodulation and treatment of neurological disorders.

articles.title: Emerging Noninvasive Approaches for the Suppression of Pathological Tremor
articles.content: Pathological tremor affects over 40 million people worldwide, significantly impairing daily activities and quality of life. Pharmacological treatments show limited efficacy, with up to 30% discontinuation rates, while surgical interventions like deep brain stimulation achieve significant tremor reduction but are often unsuitable due to age, comorbidities, or personal preference. Recently, the need for safe and effective alternatives has led to the development of innovative, noninvasive, and patient-friendly technologies for tremor management. This clinical application review analyzed 134 studies (1969-2025), categorizing them into three major modalities, focusing on their underlying neurophysiological mechanisms, with a special emphasis on the clinical perspective. The three considered modalities were force-controlling (orthoses and functional electrical stimulation), central neuromodulation (transcranial magnetic stimulation, transcranial electrical stimulation, low-intensity focused ultrasound, and transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation), and peripheral neuromodulation (afferent stimulation and vibration). Force-controlling strategies showed promising acute effects, though clinical translation remains limited by poor wearability and the development of muscle fatigue. Central neuromodulation produced moderate effects, while peripheral neuromodulation has gained clinical traction, with several devices now being commercially available. However, heterogeneity in study design, patient populations, and technology maturity remain the main obstacles for the direct comparison of techniques. Future research should prioritize larger multicenter trials, standardized outcome measures, and accessibility considerations to enable personalized, evidence-based treatment selection for diverse tremor populations.

articles.title: Assistive Trajectory Planning for Lower Limb Exoskeletons: Strategies From Laboratory-Optimized Gait to Environmentally-Adaptive Locomotion Through Multimodal Parameter Awareness
articles.content: Lower limb assistive exoskeletons (LLEs) show great potential to reduce metabolic cost, improve walking performance, and correct abnormal gait patterns. Among their core control architectures, assistive trajectory planning is key to determining system responsiveness and effectiveness under varying locomotion conditions. Many trajectory planning methods were proposed in either laboratory or unstructured real-world environments. To clarify the scope and challenges of existing research, this review categorizes trajectory planning strategies into two major types based on application scenarios: (1) strategies for laboratory settings with controllable disturbances, which usually involve optimal control for gait under stable or controllable conditions; and (2) strategies for real-world environments characterized by varying terrain, individual differences, and gait fluctuations, which usually involve adaptive control for gait under diverse or unstructured conditions. Given the foundational role of gait phase detection in trajectory planning, this review also systematically examines mainstream algorithms for gait phase recognition and estimation. Finally, the paper analyzes the limitations of existing methods and discusses the potential of advanced algorithms, intelligent multimodal sensing systems, novel sensing technologies, and embedded deployment to enhance the performance of exoskeleton assistive trajectory planning.

articles.title: A critical assessment of LGN segmentation quality based on volume, contour, and location
articles.content: Reliable segmentation of the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), a small thalamic relay nucleus essential for visual processing, is necessary for characterizing its anatomy in healthy populations and structural alterations in neurological disorders. However, accurate delineation remains challenging on routinely acquired T1-weighted images because the LGN is small, deeply located, and has limited contrast relative to surrounding thalamic tissue. Although manual segmentation remains the reference standard, it is time consuming and susceptible to rater variability, limiting its use in large datasets. Automated approaches may therefore provide a more scalable alternative. In this study, we performed a systematic benchmarking of seven automated approaches: FreeSurfer, NextBrain, DeepThalamus, HIPS-THOMAS, MASSP 2.0, BigBrain alignment, and manual novice segmentation against expert-defined ground truth. We applied a multi-metric evaluation incorporating the Dice similarity coefficient, Hausdorff distance and balanced average Hausdorff distance, volumetric similarity, and Euclidean distance. Together, these measures evaluate overlap, contour, volume, and location against expert manual segmentations. Our results indicate that HIPS-THOMAS and DeepThalamus outperformed the other automated methods in all metrics. However, manual segmentation retained high precision despite exhibiting greater inter-subject variance than the top-performing automated segmentation tools. The different metrics do not necessarily report the same order of quality, highlighting the need of using multiple metrics for evaluation segmentation quality.

articles.title: Endogenous retrovirus activation disrupts postsynaptic organization in human glutamatergic neurons
articles.content: Endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) comprise a substantial fraction of the human genome, yet whether their expression can directly alter human neuronal function remains unknown. Because glutamatergic signaling is fundamental to brain function and frequently disrupted in brain disorders, we asked whether activation of the primate-specific ERV-W group, associated with neurological disease, perturbs human glutamatergic neurons. We used CRISPR activation of the LTR17-ERV-W consensus sequence to examine its effects on neuronal and synaptic function, inducing transcription from multiple proviral loci, including five with intact open reading frames. Functionally, ERV-W activation selectively altered the postsynaptic compartment, reducing PSD-95 and NMDA receptor abundance. These changes were accompanied by altered excitatory synaptic transmission and reduced intrinsic excitability, whereas activation of ERVW-1/Syncytin-1 alone did not reproduce the phenotype. Our findings identify ERV-W activation as a modulator of human neuronal function with potential relevance to ERV-associated brain disorders.

articles.title: Human and Mouse Models of the Bipolar Disorder-Associated ANK3 p.W1989R Variant Display Altered Somatostatin Interneuron Connectivity and Function
articles.content: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a debilitating neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by recurrent mood perturbations, cognitive and functional impairment, and increased risk of suicide. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have repeatedly identified the gene ANK3, which encodes the neuronal scaffolding protein ankyrin-G, as a risk locus for BD. Ankyrin-G interacts directly with the GABAA receptor-associated protein (GABARAP) to stabilize inhibitory synapses, providing a potential mechanistic link between ANK3 variation and GABAergic dysfunction observed in BD. Previously, we identified an ANK3 p.W1989R variant in a family with BD and demonstrated that this variant abolishes the ankyrin-G/GABARAP interaction, resulting in inhibitory signaling deficits in mice. Here, we investigated the effects of this variant in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived neurons generated from an affected individual heterozygous for the ANK3 p.W1989R variant. CRISPR correction of the variant increased inhibitory synapse density on both glutamatergic and GABAergic patient-derived neurons. Integrated spatial transcriptomics and calcium imaging identified cell-type-dependent changes in gene expression and calcium dynamics. ANK3 p.W1989R somatostatin (SST) positive interneurons displayed altered calcium dynamics and reduced SST expression. To determine whether the variant impacts SST interneuron-mediated inhibition of cortical circuits, we selectively stimulated prefrontal cortical SST interneurons in heterozygous Ank3 p.W1989R mice and recorded optically evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (oIPSCs) from cortical pyramidal neurons. SST interneuron-mediated oIPSC peak amplitude, charge transfer, and decay times were reduced in variant mice, without a significant change in the paired-pulse ratio. These findings, using complementary human and mouse models, identify novel roles for ankyrin-G in SST interneuron-mediated inhibitory signaling and demonstrate that altered inhibitory connectivity and SST interneuron function are associated with ANK3 p.W1989R. This work provides mechanistic insight into how disrupted ankyrin-G-dependent synaptic function may contribute to inhibitory signaling deficits relevant to BD.

articles.title: Pediatric brain charts reveal ADHD biotypes with distinct developmental, molecular, and therapeutic profiles
articles.content: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) exhibits profound clinical heterogeneity; however, its underlying neurobiological substrates remain unclear. Here, leveraging large - scale structural magnetic resonance imaging data from 12,663 typically developing children and 1,699 children with ADHD across Chinese and United States cohorts, we construct population specific pediatric brain charts via hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling to quantify individual deviations in cortical morphology. Data-driven clustering identifies two robust, cross - ethnically replicable ADHD biotypes: an infra - normal biotype characterized by widespread cortical thinning and a supra - normal biotype marked by cortical thickening. Multivariate analyses reveal distinct brain-behavior architectures: cortical deviations correlate preferentially with symptom severity in the infra-normal biotype but with both symptom severity and cognitive performance in the supranormal biotype. Clinically, the infra-normal biotype demonstrates a superior response to methylphenidate over atomoxetine, whereas the supra-normal biotype responds comparably to both. Transcriptomic analyses identify biotype-specific molecular signatures converging with ADHD genome-wide association study (GWAS) risk loci but exhibiting distinct expression patterns in the brain. These findings classify ADHD heterogeneity into neurobiologically distinct, clinically informed biotypes, providing a mechanistic framework for precision psychiatry in pediatric ADHD.

articles.title: Unstable word form representations and greater reliance on right hemisphere during word learning in adults with a history of developmental language disorder
articles.content: Impairment in acquiring new vocabulary is a persistent deficit in developmental language disorder (DLD), but its cortical substrates remain unclear. We investigated learning of new words in young adults with DLD and typically developing (TD) control participants using magnetoencephalography (MEG). Participants were exposed to spoken real words and two sets of pseudowords, with shared beginnings, in two MEG sessions. One set of pseudowords was actively trained for three days, paired with fantasy animal pictures. Both groups learned new pseudowords, but adults with DLD recalled fewer items and confused similar sounding pseudowords more often than TD adults. MEG recordings revealed robust left temporal learning effects in both groups, along with left inferior frontal involvement. The DLD group additionally showed stronger right-hemispheric involvement and a significant right temporal learning effect for the newly learned words. Furthermore, only the DLD group showed changes in the left and right temporal responses for the real words after the learning phase, indicating altered lexical access for familiar words after integration of new word forms with overlapping phonology into the mental lexicon. Together, the findings suggest persisting problems in creating and accessing stable and distinctive phonological memory representations for word forms in adults with DLD, along with altered hemispheric balance in processing.
articles.author: Nora, A., Yan, C., Husa, V., Wilkki, V., van Vliet, M., Service, E., Salmelin, R.

articles.title: Predictive dendrites as a foundation for biological learning
articles.content: A fundamental challenge for neuroscience is to identify laws of synaptic plasticity that are consistent with experimental observations at the level of individual neurons, whilst also explaining the ability of neural networks to learn complex tasks. Here we investigate a candidate law in which neurons adjust synaptic strengths to minimize the mismatch between somatic and dendritic activity. We demonstrate that models based on this rule can effectively adjust synaptic weights across network layers to learn non-linear tasks. Moreover, minimizing mismatch between spiking activity and dendritic inputs leads to integrate-and-fire dynamics and spike-timing-dependent plasticity. The model reproduces the experimentally observed dependencies of plasticity upon initial synaptic weights and spike patterns, whilst also generating a series of testable predictions. Our results show that a single principle - minimization of somato-dendritic mismatch - links learning at the network level with fundamental properties of individual neurons, including membrane potential dynamics and canonical features of synaptic plasticity.

articles.title: NIRS-BIDS: Brain Imaging Data Structure Extended to Near-Infrared Spectroscopy
articles.content: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is an increasingly popular neuroimaging technique that measures cortical hemodynamic activity in a non-invasive and portable fashion. Although the fNIRS community has been successful in disseminating open-source processing tools and a standard file format (SNIRF), reproducible research and sharing of fNIRS data amongst researchers has been hindered by a lack of standards and clarity over how study data should be organized and stored.
